extracted.intended_audience: European patent attorneys, applicants, and EPO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evolving EPO practice on whether and how the description must be adapted to match allowable claims under Article 84 EPC, and the interplay with other EPC provisions and EPO Guidelines. Focused on prosecution-stage decisions (Rule 71(3) / Druckexemplar) and potential appeal/referral to the Enlarged Board of Appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines requirement to remove inconsistencies between claims and description
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guidelines require that the applicant remove any inconsistencies by amendment or by deleting inconsistent embodiments or marking them as not falling within the claim scope; and that general statements and claim-like clauses are deleted or amended to avoid claim-like language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the April 2023 Guidelines update, EPO examiners have taken a harder line on inconsistencies between claims and description. This may lead examiners to amend the description (or require deletion/marking of embodiments) in the Druckexemplar accompanying a Rule 71(3) EPC Communication. Applicants must consider whether to accept examiner's changes or to contest them (possibly by appeal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 84 EPC — claims must be clear, concise, and supported by the description
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 84 EPC states that 'the claims shall (i) be clear and concise and (ii) be supported by the description.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board notes that Article 84 formally places the requirement on the claims rather than on the description or drawings. This underpins questions about whether the Office can require adaptation of the description to match the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 123(2) EPC — prohibition on added subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 123(2) EPC prohibits subject-matter extending beyond the content of the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and attorneys must balance any description amendments against the risk of adding subject-matter. Decisions on what to amend/delete in the description should account for Article 123(2) constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural manifestation: Rule 71(3) EPC Druckexemplar shows examiner's proposed amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: The marked-up version of the text intended for grant (the Druckexemplar accompanying the Rule 71(3) EPC Communication) reveals the Examiner's amendments and highlights where the EPO considers adaptation necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should review the Druckexemplar to decide whether the Examiner's amendments are acceptable for grant; if not acceptable, they can request an appealable decision on the state of the file (as occurred in the cited case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delete or amend 'claim‑like' clauses and general statements in the description
rubrics_metrics.description: General statements and claim-like clauses in the description should be deleted or amended to avoid claim-like language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guidelines explicitly direct deletion or amendment of claim-like language to remove inconsistencies; applicants who retain such clauses risk the Examiner deleting them and potentially facing objections under Article 84.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity requirement interpreted as a claim‑focused standard (claims must be clear without resorting to description)
rubrics_metrics.description: A significant body of EPO case law has found that Article 84 places a requirement on the claims only, i.e., that they are clear in themselves without having to resort to the description for an interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board emphasises that 'legal certainty requires that claims are understood without having to resort to the description.' This interpretation is in tension with EPO practice that requires description adaption; it limits the degree to which the description can be used to resolve claim ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement historically required correspondence between claims and description
rubrics_metrics.description: Early case law added that the claims should correspond to, be consistent with and be commensurate with the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically this supported adaptation of the description to claims of reduced scope, but that historical approach is now questioned by the Board in light of Article 84's wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on using Article 69 EPC to justify description adaption
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 69 EPC and its interpretation (that extent of protection is determined by the claims while description/drawings are used to interpret them) have sometimes been used to justify adapting the description to claims of reduced scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board is wary of this justification, noting that 'it is not for the Office to harmonise the extent of protection conferred by the European patents [and applications] by bringing the description and/or the drawings of an application or patent in agreement with the amended claims held allowable.' Thus Article 69 should not be used to force harmonisation of description to claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question whether inconsistency between description/drawings and claims can lead to refusal under Article 84
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board formulated the question: Is there a lack of clarity of a claim or a lack of support of a claim by the description within the meaning of Article 84 EPC if a part of the disclosure (e.g., an embodiment, an example or a claim‑like clause) is not encompassed by the subject‑matter for which protection is sought ('inconsistency in scope between the description and/or drawings and the claims') and can an application consequently be refused based on Article 84 EPC if the applicant does not remove the inconsistency in scope between the description and/or drawings and the claims by way of amendment of the description ('adaption of the description')?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core legal question referred for possible further referral to the Enlarged Board; its answer will determine whether refusal for non‑adaptation is permissible and thus whether the Guidelines' approach is consistent with Article 84.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural recourse: appeal and referral to the Enlarged Board of Appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: If disagreement arises over Examiner's deletions/amendments (e.g., deletion of claim‑like clauses), an applicant may request an appealable decision on the state of the file and seek Board of Appeal review; the Board may decide to refer the legal question to the Enlarged Board of Appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A referral to the Enlarged Board would provide much‑needed clarity but would 'inevitably and significantly delay the grant' of the patent. Applicants should weigh the costs/benefits of contesting adaptions versus accepting changes to proceed to grant.
